{"basis":"measured","confidence":1.0,"fact_type":"defect","name":"MEASURED 2026-09-22: the capture-intent routing table CONTRADICTS ITSELF — row 1 sends "it must never…" to Requirement and row 7 sends "we must never…" to Constraint saying "Not a Requirement", so the rule turns on the word "it" versus "we" and flo2's sentence matches the wrong row","statement":"FOUND 2026-09-22 while lifting the routing table into the schema as data for flo2 F24 — by trying to write the rules down in a form a machine reads, which is the pass that makes a contradiction impossible to skim past.

THE TWO ROWS, verbatim from getting-started/skills/capture-intent/SKILL.md:

    row 1: "it has to…", "it must never…", "it can't take longer than…"
             -> Requirement -> add_requirement
    row 7: "we must never…", "it is not allowed to…" — a prohibition with no
           number in it
             -> Constraint -> add_constraint. **Not a Requirement.**
    row 8: a number with a unit — "under 200ms", "no more than 40kg", "£3k"
             -> Constraint

🛑 ROW 1 CLAIMS TWO PHRASINGS THAT ROWS 7 AND 8 CLAIM BACK. "it must never…" is a PROHIBITION, which row 7 routes to Constraint in bold. "it can't take longer than…" is a LIMIT, which row 8 routes to Constraint. The only thing separating row 1's prohibition from row 7's is the PRONOUN — "it" versus "we" — which is not a distinction any person or model makes reliably, and which nothing in the table says is load-bearing.

⭐ THIS IS A BETTER CAUSE FOR FLO2'S MISCLASSIFICATION THAN THE ONE REPORTED, AND IT CHANGES WHAT THE FIX HAS TO BE. F24's cause was that the rules are not served as data, so a consumer building an extraction prompt from the schema cannot see them. True, and this design was about to fix it. But flo2's actual sentence — "the water can never drop below 68 degrees" — matches row 1's "it must never…" MORE CLOSELY than row 7's "we must never…", because its subject is the thing, not the team. So THE TABLE ITSELF ROUTES IT TO REQUIREMENT. Serving the table as data, unchanged, would have served the contradiction and produced the same wrong answer with more confidence.

⇒ THE TWO DEFECTS ARE ORDERED, NOT PARALLEL. The rules must be CORRECT before being served; serving them first would have propagated a wrong rule to every consumer at once, which is worse than a wrong rule reaching one agent at a time.

WHAT THE DISTINCTION SHOULD BE, stated so the repair is not another guess — and it is already written elsewhere in this design, in capture-intent's own prose two paragraphs below the table: a Requirement states what must be DELIVERED; a Constraint BOUNDS what is allowed. The subject of the sentence is irrelevant. Row 1 should carry only delivery phrasings, and prohibition and limit phrasings belong to rows 7 and 8 whoever the sentence is about.

⚠️ AND IT EXPLAINS THE SECOND HALF OF F24 WITHOUT A NEW THEORY. `prohibition_in_prose` scans for six fixed phrasings and flo2's sentence matched none. A detector built from a table whose prohibition row is scoped to "we must never…" would naturally inherit that row's blind spot — the same wrong boundary, one instrument along. Not established: whether the detector's six were taken from this table or written separately.
